title: Why jazz began in New Orleans: dancing, race and street parades
summary: Kmen argues New Orleans' dance mania, Black dance musicians and parade bands produced jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, this will have to be very general. But, uh, anybody who wants to support the generalities, but particulars, will be able to find evidences here in the written material, at least some of the stuff I've done. Uh, one thing that I believe is easily proved is that New Orleans was a unique city in a very real sense. Different from any other American city, where the other American cities all much more like each other than any of them were like New Orleans. And I think this uniqueness, uh, as much as anything, caused jazz music to originate here, in spite of, uh, some of the current theories to the contrary. And, uh, one of the aspects of this uniqueness, uh, besides the racial mixtures, the, the cross, uh, mingling of so many different cultures, all of them bringing their music. Perhaps the easiest way they could communicate was through music at first. But one of the other and important, uh, differences was this tremendous desire for dancing here in this town. Uh, I've often thought that probably dancing grew here to be much more established as an amusement than anywhere else for probably two reasons. One was that this town was out of the way, and therefore, uh, not so easily, uh, able to get traveling, uh, entertainment, or, uh, things like that. And also not so easy for the people here to get to other towns, as for instance, the people in Philadelphia could visit New York and vice versa. And the other being that with so many different nationalities, with different languages so early here, the one kind, the one form of social amusement that they could all participate in, because no language was necessary, was dancing. But whatever the reason, dancing was a great overwhelming amusement and occupation here, with an enormous number of dance halls, both full-time and part-time. Now in the early years, the, uh, performers, teachers, the performers in the French opera, and other musicians like that, all engaged in playing for dance music. But so also did a lot of Negro bands in pre-Civil War days. But after the Civil War, uh, a certain, uh, reluctance on the part of the white professional music, uh, musicians to play, to play for dancing. And especially white men, it was considered a sort of, uh, inferior occupation for a white man to take up music. It was much better that he take up business. And, uh, uh, with the exception of the musicians in the French opera, very few white men participated in music as a livelihood. And those in the French opera were imported periodically from abroad. And yet the love for dancing carried over. And this meant that sort of by default, the trade of dance musician came more and more to be, uh, the province of the Negro, specialized in by the Negro, much as some other trades in this town, uh, such as masonry, fancy masonry, were a specialty of the Negro. And I think for this, that, that, that here is the main thing. The, uh, the Negro has the trade of playing for dancing. Dancing is extremely popular. And jazz, I think anybody would agree, was in its origins a functional music. It was a music played for dancing. Now, of course, uh, the, uh, outward forms that it would take, uh, this instrumentation, uh, in the brass, clarinet, trombone, and other brass horns, uh, was much influenced, as, again, I think is commonality, by the, uh, street marching bands that were modeled, uh, first after the French and, uh, then also after the German. As early as the 1930s, there were a number of German marching bands in the city attached to, uh, German militia. As early as what? The, the 1830s, I must say. Uh, and that is, that is European. But, again, this town was an especially crazy town for parades. Parades, uh, would, uh, be so frequent on a Sunday, spontaneous parades, that often the church couldn't get through its services if the day was nice and the doors were open. Because the bands would be, uh, out in the streets and parading around by eleven or even ten o'clock in the morning on Sundays. And this, too, goes into the stream of jazz, and I think it could be shown that while martial music was popular everywhere, nowhere in the United States were parades as popular as they were in New Orleans. Well, I see, Dick, uh, parades. Dancing. Dancing. And then the instrumentation of the French and German, uh, street bands would naturally have an influence. I should mention that in, even in pre-Civil War days, there were a great many Negro bands that paraded with, uh, militia companies or just spontaneously, as well as white bands. And, uh, there are even evidences, uh, uh, uh, in the, uh, pre-Civil War period of, uh, what today we would call a second line. Certainly great crowds often followed some of these bands, the Negro bands especially, laughing and shouting and dancing about in the streets, which implies that the music was at least, uh, lightened considerably from a ponderous kind of march. And all these things are, uh, distinctive and unique here. Uh, I think that any claim that jazz really started elsewhere, uh, is, uh, not too well supported. Now, it may be, of course, evolution of music being what it is, and jazz partaking to a great extent, uh, uh, of American characteristics and drawing in from American culture. Uh, it may well be that this music might have evolved more slowly in other places, and might have been evolving in other places, which is why I think that, uh, jazz was able to spread so rapidly. But the, uh, the birth of jazz in any recognizable form, uh, would have to, in my opinion, be placed in New Orleans.
